transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-05-04 15:23 PDT | Duration: ~52m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood PM), Priya (Helix ML), Marcus (Helix SRE), Daniel (Helix ML Eng), Sara (Helix InfoSec)

Summary (auto): quick Optimize console demo focusing on quant profiles; walked through sandbox microbench, discussed latency budget and rollback rules for exceptional hallucinations; covered security checkpoints.

00:00 Maya: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, we have Jonah and Lena with me to run through the Optimize workspace and a quick sandbox microbench focusing on int8 and fp8 tradeoffs.
00:12 Priya: hi Maya, thanks, excited. we have a fairly tight timeline, we'd like to pick a pilot config in two weeks ideally.
00:18 Maya: great noted, we'll try to make this very prescriptive. Jonah, want to take us into the console?
00:22 Jonah: yeah sure, i'll share my screen, bear with me while the console loads — okay. so this is the Optimize tab, you'll see 'profiles' at the top, we preloaded a couple of example quant profiles: int8-aggressive, int8-safe, fp8-balanced.
00:37 Marcus: quick question on naming — are these Redwood defaults or tuned per workload?
00:41 Jonah: good call — defaults are Redwood curated based on model family and typical NLU workloads; we always recommend running a microbench with your prompt set to pick the right profile. that's what the sandbox is for.
01:02 Lena: i'll add that the console shows expected percent token cost savings and an estimated latency delta at p50/p95, those numbers are extrapolated from previous runs but we surface confidence intervals.
01:17 Daniel: can you show an example microbench? we have a lot of long-context support history threads that tend to blow up latency.
01:23 Jonah: absolutely — here's the microbench runner, you can upload your prompt set or point to an S3 bucket. we seeded a synthetic dataset that includes multi-turn threads, code blocks, and numeric tables to emulate Helix traffic.
01:41 Jonah: running the INT8-aggressive profile now; note that we enable KV-cache warm starts and adaptive batching in this sandbox.
02:03 Maya: while that's running — from a decision perspective, what's the typical quality metric you look at? we usually recommend a combination: token-level perplexity shifts, and a task-specific eval like our redwood scoring harness for intent accuracy or hallucination rate.
02:19 Priya: intent accuracy matters most for us; hallucinations that invent policy or PII are show-stoppers. we also monitor tail latency for SLA.
02:28 Sara: and from security, we need to confirm no logs with unredacted PII are retained in Redwood-hosted sandboxes; also KMS integration for our production pilot.
02:38 Lena: yes, sandbox runs are ephemeral by default, and we provide an option to scrub or store encrypted artifacts. for production we support customer-managed KMS and audit logs — we'll share the docs.
02:52 Jonah: results are coming in — initial INT8-aggressive shows 42% token cost reduction, p50 latency down 18%, p95 down 9%, but we see a small uptick in hallucination flag rate for the long-context prompts.
03:14 Daniel: can you point to a specific example?
03:18 Jonah: sure, pull up failure example #7 — the model replaced a customer name with an invented company and created an action item that referenced non-existent account ids; that was 1.3% of the long-thread subset in this bench.
03:34 Priya: that 1.3 could be a big deal, what does rollback look like?
03:39 Jonah: we recommend a two-layer policy: primary profile (int8-safe or fp8-balanced) plus automatic switch rules — e.g., if hallucination detector score > threshold OR hallucination pattern matched X times in a minute, automatically route to fallback model/profile which is fp8-balanced or full fp16 hosted model. the console shows real-time failover and warm cache migration so latency hit is minimized.
04:06 Marcus: how quick is the failover? we need p95 under 800ms ideally.
04:11 Jonah: depends on model and cache; typical warm failover to fp8-balanced adds ~80–150ms at p95 in our tests for the 70B family; cold start could be larger but we have warm standby pools for Dedicated customers.
04:27 Maya: note for Dedicated you can pin capacity to keep standby ready which reduces failover time but increases cost — it's a latency vs spend tradeoff.
04:36 Daniel: what's the telemetry we get to detect these issues?
04:40 Jonah: you get per-request scoring, hallucination signals, token-level divergence heatmaps, and the ability to stream sample outputs to a secure S3 for manual review. we also include checksum diffs between profiles to spot where outputs diverge.
04:55 Sara: on the compliance side, can we keep those sample outputs encrypted and only accessible to our audit bucket?
04:59 Lena: yes — you can configure the audit bucket and KMS key in the private deployment or Dedicated account; for hosted API we offer customer-managed encryption via KMS for enterprise tiers.
05:13 Jonah: switching to fp8-balanced run now — results: ~28% token cost reduction, p50 latency down 10%, p95 basically flat vs baseline, hallucination delta negligible.
05:32 Priya: that aligns with our intuition: fp8 is safer but less cost savings. question — is there a hybrid approach where some routes use INT8 and others FP8?
05:41 Maya: absolutely — many customers use routing policies: route high-risk prompts (billing, legal, support escalation) to fp8 or hosted fp16, and route low-risk conversational queries to int8. the console makes it easy to set route rules by intent classifier or regex.
06:00 Marcus: for our architecture we prefer a single endpoint with routing upstream, can Redwood do route decisioning in the control plane rather than client side?
06:08 Jonah: yes the smart routing layer supports policy-based routing at the API gateway, so your app hits one endpoint and Redwood routes to the chosen profile/model/pool.
06:19 Daniel: curious about regression testing — if we roll out INT8, how do we ensure no silent quality regressions over time?
06:25 Lena: we recommend a continuous eval set and alerts, plus canary percentage rollouts; Optimize integrates with your CI and will surface quality drift via prompt sets and automatic scoring. you can set hard thresholds to auto-rollback.
06:41 Priya: timeline question — given our timeline, what's realistic to go pilot in 2 weeks?
06:46 Maya: if you send the prompt set and top failures today, Jonah can run the microbench and share results in 3 business days; then we schedule a 30m pilot kickoff to pick profiles and deployment mode.
06:58 Daniel: we'll try to get the set today.
07:02 Jonah: small demo follow-up — show the heatmap. here: x-axis is prompt complexity, y-axis is divergence score, color is latency. you can click any cell to see example outputs side-by-side.
07:21 Marcus: can we export the microbench results to CSV for internal cost modeling?
07:25 Jonah: yes export CSV and a prefilled cost calculator sheet.
07:31 Maya: quick pause for procurement question — there will be procurement items and a security questionnaire; Sara, are there mandatory items we should flag now?
07:38 Sara: SOC2 attestation, RBAC/SAML for console, KMS support, and data residency for EU traffic. also we need details on log retention and purge workflows.
07:50 Lena: we'll attach the SOC2 report and a document mapping Redwood controls to typical questionnaires; also the KMS integration guide.
07:59 Priya: on the long-tail prompts in the bench, could we try an alternate approach: keep INT8 but add targeted instruction tuning for hallucination-prone templates?
08:09 Jonah: yes, that's a smart strategy — targeted fine-tune or reinforcement calibration on those templates often reduces hallucination without changing bitwidth. Optimize supports running a focused evaluation after instruction tuning.
08:26 Daniel: how invasive is instruction tuning? we can't retrain core models in prod.
08:30 Jonah: we do lightweight adapters or instruction layers that sit on top; for most customers it's a small delta and reversible. we can discuss the tradeoffs if you want a separate deep dive.
08:43 Maya: okay i'm going to surface one more practical scenario — worst-case rollback during a peak incident, how do you avoid big cost spikes?
08:50 Jonah: use staged fallback: instead of switching all traffic to fp8, increase sampling for high-risk requests to fp8, divert 10% initially and monitor; if issues persist, gradually increase. console supports percentage rollouts plus automated thresholds.
09:08 Priya: that sounds reasonable.
09:12 Maya: last section — open questions and risks.
09:15 Marcus: what are the hardware assumptions? we run on A100s and some T4s for edge; will the perf numbers match?
09:20 Jonah: our baseline was A100 and H100 families for the 70B models; for T4-class hardware you should expect different latency characteristics and smaller batch efficiency; we can run a targeted bench on your hardware via a dedicated pilot.
09:36 Daniel: any known failure modes when compressing to int8? we've seen token hallucinations and numeric rounding in tables.
09:42 Jonah: yup rounding in numeric-heavy outputs is common — Optimize flags numeric drift and you can choose a higher-precision profile for numeric routes. we also surface checksum diffs to detect truncation.
09:56 Priya: final ask — please include a recommended default: for our use case (support assistant, mixed-risk intents, 99th-percentile SLA 800ms), what would Redwood recommend?
10:06 Lena: recommendation: start with fp8-balanced for baseline stability, run a focused int8-safe microbench on low-risk intents and evaluate; if int8-safe passes hallucination threshold < 0.2% and p95 under 700ms, then scale to int8 for those routes. keep an fp8 fallback with warm standby.
10:27 Maya: great — shall we recap action items? Jonah will run the microbench with your prompt set, Daniel to provide the set, Maya to send pricing and SOC/KMS docs.
10:38 Priya: ok thanks, that's actionable.
10:42 Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links to the bench, exported CSV, and the pilot proposal.
10:49 Meeting end.

Notes: transcript contains occasional ASR artifacts and shorthand; speaker turns sometimes merged. Attachments referenced: microbench-export.csv (link), SOC2_redwood.pdf (link), KMS_integration_guide.md (link).
